info.bio:
The Velvet Underground fue una banda de rock formada en Nueva York en la década del 60. Aunque nunca alcanzó el éxito comercial, es una de las bandas de rock más influyentes de la historia y posee un intenso culto, a pesar de haber durado pocos años.

Fue una de las primeras bandas en experimentar con la forma e incluir influencias avant-garde y, especialmente, el ruido de guitarras que los hizo definir el uso del noise dentro del rock.

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Lou Reed quería llevar al pop la mirada sin concesiones de Burroughs, Purdy y Selby (heroína, prostitución masculina, vida gay y travesti) y amaba el doo-wop, el R&B profundo y el «Sally Go Round the Roses» de las Jaynetts: para él la música era «la única cosa viva». John Cale venía del Dream Syndicate de La Monte Young, con sus drones meditativos; Reed ya había grabado una obra maestra del dron de una nota, «The Ostrich». Tocaban delante de películas en la Cinematheque de Jonas Mekas cuando Warhol los adoptó a finales de 1965 y Paul Morrissey les impuso como cantante a Nico, la «Pop Girl» de 1966. Su carta de presentación fue tocar ante 350 psiquiatras («un tratamiento de electroshock»); después vinieron Uptight y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable en el Dom de St Mark’s Place (abril): luces, estroboscopios, Screen Tests, bola de espejos, la danza sadomaso de Malanga y Woronov y drones a un volumen insoportable. En California chocaron con la escena local («ellos iban de ácido, nosotros de anfetamina»; Gleason los llamó camp y enfermos). Su primer single en Verve, de Tom Wilson, «All Tomorrow’s Parties» / «I’ll Be Your Mirror» (julio), un producto pop art total, no tuvo ni reseñas ni radio. Eran un espejo de la América de 1966 que casi nadie quiso mirar.
scenes.family: Vanguardia: Warhol, Velvet, free jazz, arte

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y sus herederos
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: La línea de art rock que reivindica el postpunk no es la del progresivo sinfónico sino la que va de The Velvet Underground al krautrock y al glam intelectual, fiel al principio minimalista «menos es más». Durante el «páramo» de los setenta, un racimo de espíritus afines unidos por su deuda con la Velvet (Lou Reed, John Cale, Nico, Iggy Pop, Bowie, Eno) colaboró en distintas combinaciones y sostuvo a los hipsters.
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Nueva York: la nueva bohemia
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La psicodelia de la heroína frente a la del LSD: los Velvet Underground, quizá la banda más influyente de toda la historia del rock, nacen dentro del espectáculo multimedia de Andy Warhol y fundan la vertiente «pesimista» de la psicodelia; su espíritu independiente, nihilista y subversivo se llamará punk diez años después. «Sister Ray» es, para Scaruffi, la obra maestra definitiva del rock. Alrededor: Blues Magoos, Pearls Before Swine (psych-folk de cámara), Cromagnon y los United States Of America de Joseph Byrd, pioneros de los teclados electrónicos.

scenes.name: Detroit: MC5 y Stooges
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La ciudad más industrial de EE UU y cuartel de los elementos más extremistas de la contracultura: un rock'n'roll feroz y ruidoso se convierte en la voz de los obreros y de sus hijos. Los MC5 de John Sinclair, ala revolucionaria de las revueltas estudiantiles (Kick Out The Jams, «el equivalente rockero de una explosión nuclear»); los Stooges de Iggy Pop, síntesis de Chuck Berry, Rolling Stones, Velvet Underground y Doors que inventa el punk-rock («1970») y el voodoobilly («TV Eye»). Un nuevo rock'n'roll fundado en la violencia extrema.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

scenes.name: Feedback-pop y shoegazing
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Jesus And Mary Chain acuñan el «feedback-pop»: «White Light White Heat» de la Velvet más una melodía pegadiza, o el muro de sonido de Spector con una capa de ruido de guitarra (Psychocandy). My Bloody Valentine crean algo mágico: el «shoegazing» de Kevin Shields, éxtasis y terror como dos caras de la misma luna; Loveless es la exploración definitiva de las texturas en el rock y demuestra la equivalencia entre «ruidoso» y «sinfónico». Spacemen 3 convierten el ruido sostenido en meditación zen; Loop pintan paisajes de drones.

scenes.name: Space-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Tras la orgía de distorsión del dream-pop y el shoegazing, en EE UU se busca disciplina: Mark Kramer (Shockabilly, B.A.L.L., Bongwater, el coloso The Guilt Trip); los Flaming Lips, los discípulos más locos de Pink Floyd, entre la ética punk y el burlesque hippy (Oh My Gawd, Zaireeka); Red Temple Spirits, Viv Akauldren. Galaxie 500 y Yo La Tengo, los grupos que más influirán en la década siguiente: la psicodelia como estupor exangüe (Today, On Fire) y las baladas abstractas de texturas (May I Sing With Me). Y Phish, indiferentes a la estética punk, recuperan el directo, el solo de guitarra y la improvisación colectiva.

scenes.name: Space-rock y psicodelia extrema de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fundiendo los estilos psicodélicos que preferían la jam libre (acid-rock, space-rock, raga-rock), muchos grupos esculpen empresas sonoras épicas: Fuzzhead, Crawlspace, Pressurehed, Farflung, Fuxa, Gravitar (el Metal Machine Music de Lou Reed con ritmo), Pelt, Primordial Undermind, Escapade y, por encima de todos, Bardo Pond (Bufo Alvarius, Amanita) y Hash Jar Tempo. Texas recupera la supremacía de la locura psicodélica (Ed Hall, Cherubs, ST 37, Mike Gunn, Charalambides, Linus Pauling Quartet, la Vas Deferens Organization de Dallas); San Francisco, la psicodelia ruidosa de Mason Jones (Trance, Subarachnoid Space). En Nueva Zelanda, Roy Montgomery (Dadamah, Dissolve), Dean Roberts, Flies Inside The Sun; en Japón, Kousokuya, Mainliner, Musica Transonic, Acid Mothers Temple, Ghost.

scenes.name: La segunda venida del industrial
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los noventa el estilo brutal de Nine Inch Nails lo invade todo en EE UU y el industrial se vuelve fenómeno de masas; el «aggro» de KMFDM es menos visible pero igual de ubicuo: Grotus, Filter, Stabbing Westward, Acumen, Skrew, Electric Hellfire Club, Society Burning, Gravity Kills y, lo más original, Girls Vs Boys (Venus Luxure No.1 Baby) y New Wet Kojak. La EBM internacional se vuelve más brutal (Leaether Strip, Suicide Commando, :Wumpscut:, Hocico, Mentallo & The Fixer). La «música de la fábrica de la muerte» sobrevive en los escultores de ruido: los neozelandeses Dead C (Harsh '70s Reality, «música imposible de escuchar»), Gate, Bruce Russell, Namanax, Illusion Of Safety, Maeror Tri, Towering Inferno (Kaddish). Y el «digital hardcore» de Atari Teenage Riot y Alec Empire.

podcast.title: Minimal Commercial Success (1964-1973)
podcast.body: During their nine years together, The Velvet Underground achieved "pretty much zero commercial success," selling very few records, playing sparsely attended gigs, and almost never getting airplay on underground FM radio, indicating their profound disconnect from the mainstream music industry of the time. "But in the nine years the band was together, the velvet underground had pretty much zero commercial success. They sold very few records. Their gigs were sparsely attended. And even in the era of underground FM radio almost no one played their records."

podcast.title: Appearance in 1965
podcast.body: The band first appeared in 1965 during a time when rock and roll was considered disposable, AM radio-oriented, and not "serious music." Their arrival signaled a shift towards deeper, more sophisticated, and existential music that demanded respect. "When they first appeared in 1965, rock and roll, which is what we call the singles oriented music about basically cars and girls and that sort of thing, was still largely considered to be disposable, effervescent."

podcast.title: Demo Tape Journey to UK (1965)
podcast.body: In 1965, John Cale took the Falling Spice demo tape to the United Kingdom, aiming to give it to Marianne Faithfull, Mick Jagger's partner, hoping she would pass it to Jagger or Andre Ollman (Andrew Loog Oldham) of The Rolling Stones. While the trip is confirmed, there is no evidence the tape ever left Faithfull's hands or reached Jagger. "John Kaley se la llevaría al reino unido en 1965 en uno de sus viajes para intentar darse la Marian Faithful."

podcast.title: Discovery and Patronage by Andy Warhol (December 1965)
podcast.body: One night, just as The Velvet Underground faced a second firing from Cafe Bizarre, Andy Warhol and his entourage, including groupies and "weirdos," unexpectedly visited the club. Warhol was so profoundly impressed by their "avant-garde approach to rock" that he immediately signed them to be his official house band at his performance art headquarters, The Factory, located on East 47th Street. Warhol assumed the roles of their patron, producer, and promoter, a pivotal moment that launched the band's "long, strange road to becoming legends as the first alternative rock band in history." "Andy Warhol adopts the Velvet Underground, thereby giving the band the break they needed, to eventually be hailed as the founders of alternative rock"

podcast.title: Falling Spice Demos (1965)
podcast.body: Under the name Falling Spice, the band self-produced material, including a famous demo tape recorded in their apartment in 1965. This demo featured early versions of tracks like "All Tomorrow's Parties," "Heroin," and "Venus in Furs," and represented a more intimate, poetic, and slower original vision for the band, resembling their later second album more than their debut with Nico. "con el nombre de Falling Spice ya tenemos material auto producido por ellos, tenemos esa famosa cinta pirata o esa famosa maqueta que se grabó en 1965 en su propia apartamento."

They were commissioned to perform six sets nightly, six nights a week, for five dollars per set. However, their avant-garde music often had the unintended effect of chasing away patrons rather than attracting them, leading to the band being fired at least once for driving customers away. "the band's music ten to do chase away patrons instead of luring them in and the band was fired at least once for driving away customers."

They were so far removed from the mainstream "cars and girls" music that they were signed to a jazz label because no one knew how to categorize them. "The velvet underground was not normal for 1965."

podcast.title: Early Lo-Fi Aesthetic (1966-1967)
podcast.body: The band, composed of broke musicians associated with Andy Warhol, aimed to make a record with a meager budget of possibly $1,500. Their debut album, released in March 1967, was characterized by significant hiss, distortion, recording errors, a rough final mix, and poor stereo imaging, with singer Nico often being off-key. Despite these technical flaws, the primitive sound contributed to its appeal for a segment of music fans who valued authenticity and rebellion. "The Velvet Underground's records were generally derided for sounding bad, which made all kind of sense in the late 1960s and the early 1970s because the goal back then was to achieve perfect sound or something close to it."

podcast.title: Scepter Studios Demos (1966) – Discovered by Warren Hill
podcast.body: On April 25, 1966, The Velvet Underground recorded demos at Scepter Studios in New York, resulting in two acetate test pressings that were circulated to record companies, all of whom declined to sign the band. The band later signed with Verve, re-recording their material. In 2002, Warren Hill found one of these acetates at a flea market in Chelsea, New York, for 75 cents. After researching its rarity, he auctioned it on eBay for $25,200, and it has since been digitized for wider listening. "What he had bought was one of only two copies of this test pressing. It featured the velvet underground recording some demos at Scepter Studios in New York on April 25th 1966."

xref.body: During their nine years together, The Velvet Underground achieved "pretty much zero commercial success," selling very few records, playing sparsely attended gigs, and almost never getting airplay on underground FM radio, indicating their profound disconnect from the mainstream music industry of the time. xref.title: Discovery and Patronage by Andy Warhol (December 1965)
xref.body: One night, just as The Velvet Underground faced a second firing from Cafe Bizarre, Andy Warhol and his entourage, including groupies and "weirdos," unexpectedly visited the club. Warhol was so profoundly impressed by their "avant-garde approach to rock" that he immediately signed them to be his official house band at his performance art headquarters, The Factory, located on East 47th Street. Warhol assumed the roles of their patron, producer, and promoter, a pivotal moment that launched the band's "long, strange road to becoming legends as the first alternative rock band in history." "Andy Warhol adopts the Velvet Underground, thereby giving the band the break they needed, to eventually be hailed as the founders of alternative rock"

xref.title: Early Lo-Fi Aesthetic (1966-1967)
xref.body: The band, composed of broke musicians associated with Andy Warhol, aimed to make a record with a meager budget of possibly $1,500. Their debut album, released in March 1967, was characterized by significant hiss, distortion, recording errors, a rough final mix, and poor stereo imaging, with singer Nico often being off-key. Despite these technical flaws, the primitive sound contributed to its appeal for a segment of music fans who valued authenticity and rebellion. "The Velvet Underground's records were generally derided for sounding bad, which made all kind of sense in the late 1960s and the early 1970s because the goal back then was to achieve perfect sound or something close to it."

xref.title: Scepter Studios Demos (1966) – Discovered by Warren Hill
xref.body: On April 25, 1966, The Velvet Underground recorded demos at Scepter Studios in New York, resulting in two acetate test pressings that were circulated to record companies, all of whom declined to sign the band. The band later signed with Verve, re-recording their material. In 2002, Warren Hill found one of these acetates at a flea market in Chelsea, New York, for 75 cents. After researching its rarity, he auctioned it on eBay for $25,200, and it has since been digitized for wider listening. "What he had bought was one of only two copies of this test pressing. It featured the velvet underground recording some demos at Scepter Studios in New York on April 25th 1966."

xref.body: A one-of-a-kind, undiscovered acetate pressing of the Scepter Studios Sessions for The Velvet Underground's debut album became the world's most valuable collectible alt-rock record. xref.title: Breaking Gender Barriers – First Female Rock Drummer (Retrospectively)
xref.body: When Maureen Tucker joined The Velvet Underground in 1965, there were no known women drummers in rock music; playing drums was widely considered a "man's job." She therefore broke significant gender barriers, though this pioneering role was largely unnoticed at the time, possibly due to her unconventional drumming setup. xref.title: Contrarian Persona
xref.body: Jonathan Richman, a Boston native, presented himself as the antithesis of the prevailing big names of his era. He kept his hair short, actively opposed drug use, and was frequently heard yelling "I hate hippies" around Boston. Unlike many contemporaries who favored The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, or the growing prog rock scene, Richman preferred the raw, unconventional sound of The Velvet Underground and The Stooges, leading him to be perceived as "weird" by mainstream audiences. xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

xref.body: Through his collaborations with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and his early championing of The Velvet Underground, Bowie acted as an educator in music, helping to spread awareness and appreciation for these otherwise obscure performers. xref.title: Exile and Return to Music
xref.body: After leaving The Velvet Underground, Lou Reed spent over two years in exile at his parents' house on Long Island, where he quietly focused on writing poetry. In 1972, he ended this period and released a solo album that confused his record company, but David Bowie recognized his potential. "In 1972, Lou ended his exile at his parents' house on Long Island, where he had been quietly running poetry for more than two years after stomping out on the velvet."

xref.title: Explicit Lyrics on Debut Album
xref.body: On The Velvet Underground's debut album, Lou Reed's lyrics were notably explicit, directly describing sex and drug use, specifically "heroin." This contrasted sharply with the more allusive themes of even daring hippie bands of the era, making his work shocking for 1967. "And while even the most daring hippie bands of the day were simply alluding to having sex and using drugs, Lou Reed was there actually describing it."

Their success helped popularize "alternative" as an umbrella term for distinct rock music. "I guess REM was the first and the biggest, the word alternative became more widely used as this umbrella term for rock music that was different that did not descend from the Beatles and the Stones and Led Zeppelin, but from Bowie and Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground and the Ramones."

xref.title: Fringe Status and Bowie's Admiration
xref.body: The Velvet Underground, featuring Lou Reed, occupied a position on the extreme fringes of the music scene, with little recognition outside of "Uber hipsters." Despite their obscurity, David Bowie was a great admirer of the band, particularly Lou Reed, recognizing their unique significance. "No one except the Uber hipsters gave a damn or even knew about Lou Reed in the velvet underground."

xref.title: Influence on Alt Rock
xref.body: Lou Reed's unique approach to music, particularly with The Velvet Underground, had a profound impact on the evolution of alternative rock. His unconventional vocal style and the band's subject matter — which often explored themes of sex and drugs — were considered too "weird" for mainstream audiences at the time but influenced generations of musicians. "Yet Reed's music found its way and influenced generations of musicians who'd likely idea of being weird, even if it was just for the sake of being weird."

xref.title: Influence on British Punk - Sex Pistols Connection
xref.body: Bowie's "outsider-ness," short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude endeared him to alienated working-class youth who would become the first generation of British punks. His friendships with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed (of The Velvet Underground) also made him "cool" in their eyes. Famously, on July 2nd, 1973, after Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon, a young Steve Jones (later guitarist for the Sex Pistols) stole microphones and amps from the venue, gear that would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

xref.title: New York City Origins and Controversial Subject Matter
xref.body: Emerging from the streets of New York City in 1966, The Velvet Underground, featuring Lou Reed, was deemed too unconventional for mainstream appeal. Their music, characterized by its "weirdness," openly addressed taboo subjects like sex and drugs, which were largely unaccepted in rock and roll at the time. This thematic content, more so than Lou Reed's vocal style, was a primary reason for their non-mainstream status. "Lou and the Velvet were from the streets of New York City and were just too weird for mainstream consumption."

"Lou and the Velvet were from the streets of New York City and were just too weird for mainstream consumption."

xref.title: Post-Let's Dance Audience Alienation
xref.body: Following the immense commercial success of "Let's Dance," Bowie felt a profound sense of alienation from his new audience, questioning their connection to his artistic roots. This psychological impact marked the beginning of a creative "spiral" that continued throughout the rest of the 1980s, as his subsequent work was often judged against his previous innovations. "I remember looking out over these waves of people who were coming to hear this record played live and thinking, I wonder how many velvet underground albums these people have in their record collections. I suddenly felt very apart from my audience, and it was depressing because I didn't know what they wanted."

xref.title: Sterling Morrison's Academic Pursuits and Diverse Careers
xref.body: Sterling Morrison began his academic journey as an English major at Syracuse University, where he met Lou Reed. Though he did not graduate at that time, he completed his studies at City College in New York City in 1970. Following the official end of The Velvet Underground a year later, he enrolled at the University of Texas at Austin, where he earned a PhD in medieval studies. He then secured a teaching position in Texas until the mid-1980s. "Sterling was an English major at Syracuse University, which is where he met Lou Reed."

xref.body: Around the time The Velvet Underground, The Stooges, MC5, and Captain Beefheart were making records, David Bowie was struggling to define his own image, style, and sound, without much success. "Well, he was trying to find himself. He was trying to come up with an image and a style and a sound that would work for him and he wasn't doing very well."

xref.title: Unconventional Drumming Style
xref.body: Moe Tucker, the original drummer for The Velvet Underground, developed a distinctive and unconventional drumming style. She played standing up, primarily used mallets instead of sticks, and notably played a bass drum positioned on its side, employing marching band drums or a timpani. Her approach focused on keeping time and providing deep rhythmic backing, which was visually striking and subtle yet mesmerizing on recordings. "Mot wasn't exactly what you would call a conventional rock drummer. First of all, she played standing up. She played mostly with mallets, not sticks. There was a snare drum and a couple of tom-toms, but no symbols. And most striking of all, her bass drum was on its side."

xref.title: Unheard-of Female Drummer - Mo Tucker
xref.body: The Velvet Underground featured Mo Tucker as their drummer, a significant anomaly in the mid-1960s when having a female drummer in a rock band was virtually unheard of. "They had a female drummer, something that was unheard of in the middle 1960s."

xref.title: Velvet Spider Genus
xref.body: In 2012, an international group of biologists discovered a new genus of velvet spider that, unlike its relatives, lives underground. This discovery led to the species being named *luregia anulepis*, directly inspired by the band's name and its connection to the song "Tomorrow's Parties." "Luread and the velvet underground, the inspiration for the scientific name given to a particular type of velvet spider that lives underground."

xref.title: Václav Havel and The Velvet Revolution Influence
xref.body: Václav Havel, a Czech rock fan and dissident, was greatly inspired by The Velvet Underground, and the treatment of the Plastic People of the Universe motivated him into politics. He later named the non-violent transition from communism to democracy in Czechoslovakia the "Velvet Revolution," and was elected president of the Czech Republic on January 26, 1993. "The band's very existence was inspired by the Velvet Underground. The way the band was treated outraged Havol, who was driven into politics."

xref.title: World's First True Alternative Band (Late 1960s-Early 1970s)
xref.body: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, The Velvet Underground, led by Lou Reed, was recognized as potentially the world's first true alternative band. Their music was characterized by kinky themes, delving into topics of "weird sex and drugs and rock and roll." "Through the late 60s and early 70s, Lou was the leader of the Velvet Underground, which might have been the world's first true alternative band."
